title: Genetically Modified Organisms and Modern Biotechnology
subtitle: Understand how GM crops are made, weigh the real evidence on safety, environment and cost, and lead calm, accurate conversations about GMOs in your community.
description: An advanced literacy course on genetic modification for African women who farm, feed families or lead groups. You learn the biology behind GM crops, how WHO and Codex approach food safety, the real environmental and economic questions, and how Nigeria's National Biosafety Management Agency regulates GMOs. You finish with a country brief, a fully evaluated claim and a community outreach plan.
outcomes: Explain DNA, genes, transformation, events and genome editing in plain language
Interpret a GM food safety comparison and state accurately what WHO concludes
Calculate refuge areas and compare seed and spray costs for an informed farm decision
Describe how the Cartagena Protocol, Codex and Nigeria's NBMA fit together, and comment on a public display notice
Score any GMO claim with a five-question method and write a fair verdict
Plan and run a balanced 30-minute community conversation on GM food and farming
audience: Women farmers, cooperative and group leaders, teachers, health workers and food traders who want accurate, balanced knowledge of GMOs to guide their own decisions and their communities.
tools: A smartphone with internet access for the NBMA website and WHO pages
A notebook or phone notes app for your claims log
Flip chart paper or printed handouts for a community session

modules.title: How Genetic Modification Really Works
modules.overview: This module builds the science you need before any debate makes sense: what DNA, genes and proteins do, how scientists move one gene into a crop, and which traits GM crops actually carry. You finish by sorting the claims you have heard into clear types so you know which evidence each one needs.

lessons.title: DNA, genes and the meaning of modern biotechnology
objectives: Explain how DNA, genes and proteins produce a visible trait
State the WHO definition of a genetically modified organism in your own words
Tell traditional biotechnology apart from modern biotechnology using everyday examples
Recognise GM products that are already common in medicine and food processing

blocks.text: Every living thing, from a cowpea plant to a goat to the yeast that raises your bread, carries a set of instructions written in **DNA**. DNA is a long chain made of four chemical letters, usually written **A, T, G and C**. The order of these letters is the message. A stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for one job is called a **gene**.

blocks.name: dna-double-helix
blocks.caption: DNA is the instruction book; a gene is one recipe inside it.

blocks.text: Most genes are recipes for **proteins**. Proteins do the work in a cell. Some proteins build structures, some speed up chemical reactions, some carry signals. The colour of a maize grain, a cowpea's ability to fix nitrogen, or a plant's response to drought all come from proteins made from genes, working together with the environment the plant grows in.

blocks.title: From DNA to a trait you can see
blocks.caption: A change in the DNA letters can change the protein, and so change the trait.

blocks.text: What makes an organism genetically modified

The World Health Organization (WHO) defines genetically modified organisms (GMOs) as organisms, meaning plants, animals or microorganisms, in which the DNA has been altered **in a way that does not occur naturally by mating and/or natural recombination**. The key idea is the method. When two cowpea plants cross in a field, their genes mix, but that is natural mating, so the offspring is not a GMO. When a scientist inserts a chosen gene into a cowpea cell in a laboratory, the result is a GMO.

This also explains why a GMO can carry a gene from a very different living thing. Mating can only mix genes between closely related plants. Laboratory methods can move a gene from a soil bacterium into a plant, because DNA uses the same four letters in all living things, and the plant cell can read a bacterial recipe once it is placed correctly.
Traditional and modern biotechnology

**Biotechnology** simply means using living things or their parts to make products. By that meaning, Nigerian women have practised biotechnology for generations. **Modern biotechnology** is the newer set of laboratory tools that work directly on DNA, such as recombinant DNA (joining DNA from different sources) and genome editing. Regulators, including Nigeria's biosafety law, focus on modern biotechnology and its products.

head: Type
What happens
Familiar examples
rows: Natural microbes or selected plants and animals do the work; no direct change to DNA
Fermenting ogi or garri, brewing pito, making yoghurt, raising bread with yeast, selecting the best seed to replant
A chosen gene is cut out, joined to control signals and placed into a new organism
Insulin for diabetes made by microbes, GM crops such as insect-resistant (Bt) varieties
A tool such as CRISPR changes a few letters in the organism's own DNA at a chosen spot
Newer crop and animal research; how it is regulated differs from country to country

blocks.text: Many people are surprised to learn that GM products already sit quietly in daily life. Human insulin used by many people with diabetes is made by genetically modified microorganisms that carry the human insulin gene. Much of the cheese made around the world uses an enzyme called chymosin produced by GM microbes instead of taking it from calves' stomachs. These uses rarely cause public argument, which shows that the debate is usually about particular crops, companies and decisions, not about the science of DNA itself.

blocks.title: Worked example: sorting products into the right category
blocks.context: For example, Amaka, a secondary school biology teacher in Enugu, prepares a short sorting exercise for her women's group before a discussion on GM foods.
steps: She lists six items: ogi, yoghurt, seed she selected from her best cowpea plants, human insulin, cheese made with microbial chymosin, and an insect-resistant GM cowpea.
She asks for each item: did people change the DNA directly in a laboratory? If no, it is traditional biotechnology or ordinary breeding.
Ogi, yoghurt and selected seed answer no: 3 items are traditional.
Insulin, microbial chymosin and GM cowpea answer yes: 3 items come from modern biotechnology.
She points out that only one of the 3 modern items is a living crop planted in fields, which is why it faces environmental review as well as food review.
blocks.result: The group sees that 3 of 6 everyday items involve modern biotechnology, and that the method of change, not the name of the food, decides the category.

blocks.title: Hybrid is not the same as GM
blocks.text: Hybrid seed comes from crossing two chosen parent lines by pollination. No gene is inserted in a laboratory, so a hybrid is not a GMO. A GM variety can also be a hybrid if the inserted gene is bred into hybrid parents, so always ask how the variety was made.

Keep this lesson's core idea in mind for the whole course. A GMO is defined by **how** its DNA was changed. Whether a particular GMO is safe, useful, fairly priced or legal to plant are separate questions, and each needs its own evidence. The rest of this course gives you the tools to answer each one carefully.

takeaways: DNA is written in four letters; a gene is a recipe, usually for a protein.
WHO defines a GMO by the method: DNA altered in a way mating and natural recombination cannot achieve.
Fermenting ogi is traditional biotechnology; inserting a gene is modern biotechnology.
GM microbes already make insulin and cheese enzymes; most debate is about specific crops.

activity.title: Biotechnology in your kitchen
steps: List eight foods, drinks or medicines you use in a normal week.
For each, write whether it involves no biotechnology, traditional biotechnology or modern biotechnology.
For any item you are unsure about, write the question you would need answered (for example, how was this enzyme made?).
Explain to one family member, in two sentences, the difference between a hybrid and a GM crop.
activity.evidence: Your eight-item table with categories and open questions, plus a one-line note of how the explanation went.

lessons.title: Building a GM crop: genes, transformation and genome editing
objectives: Describe the parts of a gene construct: promoter, trait gene and marker
Explain the two main ways genes are moved into plant cells
Calculate how backcrossing brings a new trait into a local variety
Distinguish transgenic modification from genome editing

blocks.text: Making a GM crop is slow, careful work that usually takes many years from the first idea to seed in a farmer's hand. This lesson walks through the main steps using the best-known example in Africa: crops that carry a gene from the soil bacterium ***Bacillus thuringiensis***, shortened to **Bt**.

blocks.name: woman-microscope
blocks.alt: A woman scientist looking into a microscope
blocks.caption: Plant transformation happens in single cells grown in the laboratory before any plant reaches a field.

blocks.text: Step 1: choose the gene

Bt bacteria make proteins called **Cry proteins**. A Cry protein is harmless to most animals, but when a specific group of insect larvae eat it, the protein is activated in their gut, binds to particular receptors on the gut wall and damages it, so the larva stops feeding and dies. Each Cry protein affects a narrow group of insects. Bt sprays made from the bacteria have long been used by farmers, including organic farmers. In a Bt crop, the plant itself makes the Cry protein, so the larva meets it when it bites the plant.

For example, Nigeria's biosafety regulator has published an application for a GM cowpea containing the **Cry2Ab** gene, which gives resistance to the **Maruca pod borer**, a caterpillar that bores into cowpea flowers and pods.
Step 2: build the gene construct

A gene on its own does nothing in a new organism. Scientists join it to control signals. The **promoter** is the on-switch that tells the plant where and how strongly to use the gene. The **trait gene** is the recipe itself, often adjusted so the plant reads it efficiently. A **marker gene** lets scientists find the few cells that took up the construct. This whole package is the **construct**.

blocks.title: How a GM crop is made
blocks.caption: Each step filters out failures, so only a few plants from thousands of cells go forward.

blocks.text: Step 3: transform plant cells

items: **Agrobacterium method:** *Agrobacterium tumefaciens* is a soil bacterium that naturally transfers a piece of its DNA into plant cells. Scientists remove the disease-causing genes and use it as a delivery vehicle for the construct.
**Gene gun (biolistics):** tiny gold or tungsten particles coated with DNA are fired into plant tissue, and some cells take the DNA into their own.
After either method, the cells are grown on a nutrient gel (tissue culture). The marker helps keep only transformed cells, which are regrown into whole plants.

blocks.text: Each time the construct lands in a plant's DNA, it lands in one particular place. That single, specific insertion is called an **event**. Different events of the same gene can behave differently, so developers compare many events and keep the one with stable, useful expression and no obvious side effects. Regulators approve a named event, not a gene in general. That is why the Nigerian cowpea application refers to **Event 245F**.
Step 4: breed the trait into varieties farmers want

The event is usually first made in a variety that is easy to transform, not the variety farmers prefer. Breeders then use **backcrossing**: they cross the GM plant with a popular local variety, select offspring carrying the gene, cross those back to the local variety again, and repeat. Each backcross halves the share of DNA still coming from the transformation parent.

blocks.title: Worked example: how many backcrosses are needed?
blocks.context: For example, a breeding team wants a GM cowpea line that is at least 95 percent the same as a local variety farmers already like for its grain colour and cooking quality.
steps: First cross (GM line x local variety): on average 50 percent of the DNA comes from the local variety.
Backcross 1: half of the remaining 50 percent is replaced, so 50 + 25 = 75 percent local.
Backcross 2: 75 + 12.5 = 87.5 percent local.
Backcross 3: 87.5 + 6.25 = 93.75 percent local, still below 95.
Backcross 4: 93.75 + 3.125 = 96.875 percent local, which passes the 95 percent goal.
At each generation they keep only plants that still carry the Bt gene, checked with a laboratory test.
blocks.result: Four backcrosses after the first cross give about 96.9 percent local DNA on average. With one cowpea generation per season, this is one reason GM varieties take years to reach farmers.

blocks.text: Genome editing is a different tool

**Genome editing**, for example with **CRISPR-Cas9**, works like a find-and-replace tool. A guide molecule finds an exact spot in the plant's own DNA and an enzyme cuts it there. When the cell repairs the cut, a few letters can be changed, switched off or replaced. Often no foreign gene remains in the final plant. Because of this, countries are still deciding how to treat edited crops: some regulate them like GMOs, some treat certain edits like conventional breeding. Always check the current rule in your own country rather than assuming.

blocks.title: Never plant seed of unknown origin
blocks.text: Seed passed hand to hand and described as a new improved or GM variety may be unapproved, mislabelled or fake. Planting unapproved GM material is against the law in countries with biosafety laws, and fake seed can ruin a season. Buy only labelled, certified seed from registered dealers.

takeaways: Bt crops make a Cry protein that targets a narrow group of insect larvae.
A construct joins a promoter, a trait gene and a marker; one insertion is called an event.
Agrobacterium and the gene gun are the two classic delivery methods.
Backcrossing adds the trait to a local variety; four backcrosses give about 97 percent local DNA.
Genome editing changes the plant's own DNA, and rules for it differ between countries.

activity.title: Explain the journey of a GM seed
steps: Draw the six-step flow from this lesson on one page, in your own words.
Under each step, write one sentence about why it is needed.
Repeat the backcross calculation for a 99 percent goal and record how many backcrosses are needed.
Write two sentences explaining to a farmer why an approval names a specific event.
activity.evidence: A photo of your drawn flow chart and your written backcross calculation.

lessons.title: GM traits, Africa's crops and auditing the claims you have heard
objectives: Name the main trait groups found in GM crops and what each does
Connect GM traits to real pest and climate problems in Nigerian farming
Sort GMO claims into food safety, environmental, economic and legal types
Set up a personal claims log to use through the rest of the course

blocks.text: The word GMO covers many different products. A cotton plant that resists bollworms and a rice plant that makes a vitamin precursor have almost nothing in common except the method used to make them. Good literacy starts by asking: **which crop, which trait, which event, and which country?**

blocks.name: ear-of-maize
blocks.caption: Maize, cotton and cowpea are the crops most often discussed in African GM research.

blocks.text: The main trait groups

head: Trait group
What it does
Example problem it targets
rows: Plant makes a Cry protein toxic to specific caterpillars or beetles
Maruca pod borer in cowpea; bollworms in cotton; stem borers and fall armyworm in maize
Plant survives a specific weedkiller that kills surrounding weeds
Weed control with less hand weeding
Plant keeps yielding better under water stress
Plant resists a specific virus or disease
Viral diseases that wipe out a crop
Plant makes more of a nutrient
Golden Rice was engineered to produce beta-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A

blocks.text: In Nigeria, the National Biosafety Management Agency (NBMA) has published notices about insect-resistant cowpea and about **TELA maize**, which it described as resistant to fall armyworm and stem borer and tolerant of drought. These crops target pests that Nigerian farmers already fight with repeated spraying or heavy losses. Whether a particular variety is approved and on sale in your area at a given time is something you check with NBMA and your extension office, not something to assume.

Notice that a trait solves one named problem, not every problem. A Bt cowpea that resists Maruca pod borer still needs protection from other pests, good spacing, weeding and proper drying after harvest. A drought-tolerant maize still yields less in a drought than in a good season; it simply tends to lose less. When someone describes a GM crop as a complete answer, ask which pest or stress it targets and what it leaves untouched.

Also remember that the same trait can be placed in many different crops and varieties, and that the event, the variety and the country all matter. A trait that has been approved in one country may not be approved in its neighbour, and an event approved for food import may not be approved for planting.
Four types of claim

Most confusion comes from mixing up different kinds of question. Someone may say "GMOs are bad" when they really mean "I am worried big seed companies will control farmers". That is a real concern, but it is an economic question, not a food safety question. Answering it with food safety evidence, or the other way round, goes nowhere.

blocks.title: Four kinds of GMO claim
items: Food safety: is it safe to eat?
Environment: effects on insects, weeds, wild plants
Law and policy: approved, labelled, regulated?
axes: About people or about the wider system
About health or about money and rules
blocks.caption: Each type of claim needs a different kind of evidence and a different expert.

items: **Food safety claims** need evidence from food safety assessments and health bodies such as WHO and Codex.
**Environmental claims** need field studies and environmental risk assessments for that crop in that place.
**Economic claims** need farm records, seed prices, yield data and market information.
**Legal and policy claims** need the actual law and the regulator's published decisions.

blocks.title: Worked example: auditing a WhatsApp voice note
blocks.context: For example, Halima, who runs a grain stall in Kano, receives a long voice note from a cousin. She writes down every separate claim it makes and sorts them.
steps: Claim A: "GM beans will damage your womb." Type: food safety (health). Source given: none.
Claim B: "Bees and butterflies will all die." Type: environment. Source given: none.
Claim C: "Farmers will have to buy seed every season." Type: economics. Source given: none, but she knows hybrid seed already works this way.
Claim D: "The government has banned all GM crops." Type: law. She can check this directly on the NBMA website.
She counts: 4 claims, 4 different types, 0 sources named.
blocks.result: Halima now has four precise questions to check instead of one vague fear. Claim D can be checked today on the regulator's website, and the others will be examined in Module 2.

blocks.title: Write the claim word for word
blocks.text: When you log a claim, copy its exact words and note where you met it and the date. Claims change as they are forwarded. Exact wording lets you see whether the original message really said what people now repeat.
Your claims log

Through this course you will keep a simple claims log in a notebook or a phone note. Use five columns: the claim in exact words, where you met it, its type, the source it gives, and what you later found. You will return to this log in every module, and it becomes part of your final project.

Be honest with yourself as you fill it. Include claims you have believed as well as ones you doubt, and claims that favour GMOs as well as ones against them. A literate person checks a claim she likes with the same care as one she dislikes.

takeaways: Always ask: which crop, which trait, which event, which country?
Main trait groups: insect resistance, herbicide tolerance, drought tolerance, disease resistance, nutrition.
Separate food safety, environmental, economic and legal claims; each needs its own evidence.
Keep a claims log with exact wording, source, type and what you found.

activity.title: Start your claims log
steps: Create a five-column log: exact claim, where and when you met it, type, source given, what you found.
Add at least six claims about GMOs you have heard, including at least two that are in favour of GMOs.
Label each with one of the four types.
Circle one legal claim you can check this week on the NBMA website.
activity.evidence: A photo or screenshot of your claims log with at least six classified entries.

quiz.q: According to the WHO definition, which of these is a genetically modified organism?
options: A hybrid maize from crossing two inbred lines
A cowpea plant that received a bacterial gene in a laboratory
Seed selected from the best plants in a farm
quiz.explain: WHO defines a GMO by DNA being altered in a way that does not occur naturally through mating or natural recombination. Laboratory gene insertion does that; crossing, fermenting and selecting do not.

quiz.q: A regulator approves 'Event 245F'. What does the word 'event' refer to?
options: The date of the approval meeting
One specific insertion of the gene construct in the plant's DNA
quiz.explain: Each insertion lands in one place in the plant's DNA. That specific insertion is an event, and approvals name the event because different events can behave differently.

quiz.q: How does a Bt protein kill a target caterpillar?
options: It poisons the soil around the plant
It makes the leaves too hard to chew
It is activated in the larva's gut, binds specific receptors and damages the gut wall
quiz.explain: Cry proteins are activated in the gut of specific insect larvae and bind receptors there. Most other animals lack those receptors, which is why each Cry protein has a narrow target range.

quiz.q: A breeding line starts at 50 percent local DNA after the first cross. On average, what percentage is local after three backcrosses?
quiz.explain: Each backcross halves the remaining non-local share: 50, then 75, then 87.5, then 93.75 percent after the third backcross.

quiz.q: Someone says, 'GM crops will make farmers depend on seed companies.' What type of claim is this?
quiz.explain: It is about cost, seed supply and market power, so it is economic. It needs farm and market evidence, not food safety studies.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between genome editing and transgenic modification?
options: Genome editing always adds a gene from another species
Genome editing is the same as hybrid breeding
Genome editing changes letters at a chosen spot in the organism's own DNA, often leaving no foreign gene
Genome editing only works on animals
quiz.explain: Tools like CRISPR cut at a precise place in the organism's own DNA so a few letters can be changed. Transgenic methods insert a gene construct, often from another species.

modules.title: Evidence, Risk and Regulation
modules.overview: This module looks at the evidence behind the three biggest questions: is GM food safe to eat, what happens in the field and on the farm, and who decides what may be planted. You will learn how food safety assessment works, the real environmental and economic issues, and how international rules and Nigeria's biosafety law fit together.

lessons.title: How GM food safety is assessed and what WHO concludes
objectives: List the six areas WHO says a GM food safety assessment covers
Explain the comparative approach used in Codex guidelines
Read a simple compositional comparison and judge whether a difference matters
State accurately what WHO says, and does not say, about GM food safety

blocks.text: When people ask "Is GM food safe?", scientists answer with a narrower question: **is this particular food, from this particular event, as safe as the conventional food it replaces?** That question can be tested. It is the basis of international guidance agreed by governments through the **Codex Alimentarius Commission**, the joint body of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and WHO that sets international food standards.

blocks.name: test-tube
blocks.caption: Food safety assessment compares the GM food with its conventional counterpart, one property at a time.

blocks.text: The six areas WHO lists
WHO explains that safety assessment of GM foods generally looks at:

items: **Toxicity:** direct health effects of the new protein or any changed substances.
**Allergenicity:** whether the food could provoke an allergic reaction.
**Specific components** thought to have nutritional or toxic properties.
**Stability of the inserted gene** over generations.
**Unintended effects:** any change nobody planned, found by comparing the GM and conventional plant.

blocks.text: The comparative approach

Codex guideline CXG 45-2003, on food safety assessment of foods from recombinant-DNA plants, uses a **comparator**: the conventional version of the same crop with a history of safe use. Developers grow the GM plant and its comparator side by side and measure nutrients, natural toxins and anti-nutrients. Differences are then examined: is the difference large, is it outside the normal range seen in ordinary varieties, and could it affect health?

blocks.title: Comparative safety assessment
blocks.caption: Every difference found sends the assessor back to look more closely before a decision is made.

blocks.text: For the new protein itself, assessors check whether it resembles known toxins or allergens, how quickly it breaks down in digestion-like conditions, and how much of it is present in the part people eat. Eating DNA is not a risk in itself: people eat the DNA of every plant and animal in their diet daily, and digestion breaks it down. The question is always what the new protein and any unintended changes do.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a compositional comparison
blocks.context: For example, a study summary for an illustrative GM cowpea lists protein content per 100 g of dry grain for the GM line, its conventional comparator, and the range found across many ordinary cowpea varieties. The numbers below are for practice only.
steps: GM line: 24.1 g protein. Comparator: 23.5 g protein. Normal range in ordinary varieties: 20.0 to 28.0 g.
Difference: 24.1 minus 23.5 = 0.6 g.
Percentage difference: 0.6 divided by 23.5 = 0.0255, about 2.6 percent.
Check the range: 24.1 lies between 20.0 and 28.0, so it is normal for cowpea.
Now suppose a natural anti-nutrient were 40 percent higher and outside the normal range. That would need explanation and possibly more testing before approval.
blocks.result: A 2.6 percent difference inside the normal range is not a safety concern on its own. Assessors care about differences that are large, outside natural variation or biologically meaningful.

blocks.text: Allergy checks deserve special attention because allergies can be severe. Assessors ask whether the gene came from a source known to cause allergies, whether the new protein's sequence resembles any known allergen, and whether it survives digestion. If a protein raised a real allergy concern, the product would not be expected to pass, which is the purpose of checking before release rather than after.
What WHO actually concludes

WHO's public guidance states that **GM foods currently available on the international market have passed safety assessments and are not likely to present risks for human health**. Read the sentence carefully. It covers foods that have passed assessment. It does not say every possible GM food is safe, and WHO adds that each GM food should be assessed case by case. That is exactly why assessment and regulation exist.

head: Statement
Supported by WHO guidance?
rows: Approved GM foods on the market are not likely to present risks to health
Every GM food is automatically safe
No: each must be assessed case by case
GM foods are proven to cause disease
No: approved foods passed safety assessment
Labelling rules are the same everywhere
No: WHO notes there is no worldwide consensus on labelling

blocks.title: Food safety still applies to every food
blocks.text: Whether a grain is GM or not, the everyday hazards remain: mould and aflatoxin in badly dried maize and groundnuts, pesticide residues when spraying rules are ignored, and weevil-damaged grain. Dry grain well, store it off the floor in clean bags, and never eat seed that has been treated with chemicals.

Honest literacy holds both halves together. The weight of evidence reviewed by health bodies supports the safety of approved GM foods, and good regulation still matters because new products must earn that conclusion one at a time.

takeaways: Safety is judged product by product against a conventional comparator.
WHO lists toxicity, allergenicity, key components, gene stability, nutrition and unintended effects.
A difference inside the normal range of ordinary varieties is not a concern on its own.
WHO: GM foods on the international market passed assessment and are not likely to present health risks.

activity.title: Practise reading a comparison
steps: Copy the worked example numbers and recalculate the difference and percentage on your phone calculator.
Invent a second line: fibre 15.0 g in the GM line, 16.2 g in the comparator, normal range 12.0 to 18.0 g. Calculate the difference and decide whether it is within range.
Write WHO's safety sentence word for word and underline the words that limit what it covers.
Add one food safety claim from your claims log and note what this lesson tells you about it.
activity.evidence: Your two calculations, the underlined WHO sentence and your updated claims log entry.

lessons.title: Environment and farm economics: resistance, gene flow and seed costs
objectives: Explain how pests and weeds can evolve resistance to GM traits
Plan a refuge area from a stewardship percentage
Describe gene flow and the questions it raises for wild relatives and seed saving
Weigh seed price against reduced spraying in a simple farm comparison

blocks.text: Food safety is only one part of the GMO question. The more open debates, and the ones that matter most to farmers, are about what happens in the field and in the farm account book. These are real issues, and a balanced person can discuss them without exaggeration in either direction.

blocks.name: lady-beetle
blocks.caption: Environmental review asks how a GM crop affects insects it was not designed to target.

blocks.text: Resistance: the trait can wear out

Insects and weeds evolve. If a field of Bt plants kills almost every pod borer, the rare larva that carries a natural resistance gene survives, mates with another survivor and passes resistance on. Within some seasons the trait stops working. Insect resistance to Bt crops and weed resistance to herbicides have been reported in several countries where stewardship was weak. WHO also lists effects on non-target organisms and gene escape among the environmental issues assessed.

The main defence for Bt crops is a **refuge**: an area of non-Bt plants of the same crop planted near the Bt field. Susceptible insects survive in the refuge and mate with any rare resistant insects from the Bt field, so their offspring stay susceptible. The refuge size and layout are set in the stewardship guide that comes with the seed, so always follow that guide.

blocks.title: How a refuge slows resistance
blocks.caption: Without the refuge, survivors mate with each other and resistance builds quickly.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a refuge
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi farms 2 hectares in Benue and buys certified Bt cowpea seed. Suppose the stewardship leaflet with her seed says 20 percent of her cowpea area must be refuge planted with non-Bt cowpea. The 20 percent is used here only for practice; her real figure comes from her own leaflet.
steps: Total cowpea area: 2 hectares = 20,000 square metres.
Refuge: 20 percent of 20,000 = 0.20 x 20,000 = 4,000 square metres.
Bt area: 20,000 minus 4,000 = 16,000 square metres.
Her field is 100 m wide, so a refuge strip along one side is 4,000 divided by 100 = 40 m deep.
She marks the strip with pegs before planting and writes the layout in her farm notebook.
blocks.result: Ngozi plants 16,000 square metres of Bt cowpea and a 40 m by 100 m strip (4,000 square metres) of non-Bt cowpea as refuge.

blocks.text: Stewardship is a shared job. One farmer who skips the refuge weakens the trait for every neighbour growing the same crop, because insects fly between farms. This is why cooperatives and extension officers often discuss refuge rules as a group, and why a farmer who buys GM seed should read and keep the stewardship leaflet as carefully as the seed label.
Gene flow and seed saving

Pollen moves by wind and insects. **Gene flow** is when pollen from a GM crop fertilises a neighbouring plant, either a non-GM field of the same crop or a wild relative. Risk assessors ask whether the crop has wild relatives in the area, whether the trait would give those relatives an advantage, and how far pollen travels. These are local questions, which is why environmental assessment is done country by country. Gene flow also matters to farmers who save seed or sell to buyers that demand non-GM grain.
The farm account book

Economic claims cut both ways. GM seed may cost more, may come with stewardship rules, and in some systems is sold under licence. On the other hand, an insect-resistant crop can need fewer insecticide sprays, which saves chemical, labour and the farmer's own exposure to poison. The honest answer depends on the actual seed price, pest pressure and spraying practice on that farm.

In this illustrative table the Bt crop costs more for seed but less overall. Change the numbers and the answer changes: if pod borer pressure is low and the farmer only sprays twice anyway, conventional seed is cheaper. Use your own records, not someone else's average.

blocks.title: Pesticide safety does not disappear
blocks.text: A Bt crop controls only its target pests. If you still spray for other insects, wear gloves, long sleeves, boots and a face covering, never spray into the wind, keep children away, observe the waiting period on the label before harvest, and never store chemicals in food or drink containers.

takeaways: Pests and weeds can evolve resistance; stewardship slows it.
A refuge of non-Bt plants keeps the pest population susceptible; follow the size in your seed's guide.
Gene flow questions are local: wild relatives, pollen distance, seed saving and buyers.
Compare seed cost with spray savings using your own farm numbers.

activity.title: Run the numbers for your situation
steps: Choose a crop area you know (your farm, a relative's, or 1 hectare as a practice case).
Calculate a refuge using 10 percent and then 20 percent of that area, in square metres.
Fill in a seed plus spray table using prices you collect from a local agro-dealer, marked as approximate.
Write two sentences on which option would be cheaper and what would change that answer.
activity.evidence: Your refuge calculations and the completed cost table with your dated price notes.

lessons.title: Who decides: the Cartagena Protocol, Codex and Nigeria's NBMA
objectives: Explain what the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety and Codex each cover
Describe the role of Nigeria's National Biosafety Management Agency
Follow an NBMA public display notice and plan a comment within the deadline
Find current approval information for your own country

blocks.text: No single world authority approves GM crops. Instead, international agreements set shared principles, and each country's own law and regulator decide what may be imported, tested or planted. Knowing which body does what lets you check claims about the law quickly and accurately.

blocks.name: woman-scales
blocks.alt: A woman holding the scales of justice
blocks.caption: Biosafety law balances potential benefits against possible risks to health and the environment.

blocks.text: The international layer

items: **Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety:** adopted on 29 January 2000 as a supplementary agreement to the Convention on Biological Diversity. It aims to protect biological diversity from potential risks of living modified organisms from modern biotechnology. It sets an **advance informed agreement** procedure, so a country gets the information it needs before agreeing to import such organisms, and it created the **Biosafety Clearing-House**, an online system for sharing information.

**Codex Alimentarius:** the joint FAO and WHO food standards body. Its texts include CXG 44-2003, Principles for the Risk Analysis of Foods Derived from Modern Biotechnology, and CXG 45-2003 on safety assessment of foods from recombinant-DNA plants, plus a compilation of texts relevant to labelling.
**Labelling:** WHO notes there is no worldwide consensus on labelling and traceability of GM foods, so rules differ from country to country.

blocks.text: The Nigerian layer

In Nigeria, the regulator is the **National Biosafety Management Agency (NBMA)**, established under the National Biosafety Management Agency Act, signed in April 2015. The agency describes its mandate as providing a regulatory framework to safeguard human health and the environment from potential adverse effects of modern biotechnology and its products, while harnessing their potential for the benefit of Nigerians. It regulates the release into the environment, handling and use of GMOs, and it acts against unauthorised material: for example, it has publicised the disposal of unauthorised transgenic cotton seed.

The Act requires **public display** of applications for permits to intentionally release a GMO, so citizens can give input before a decision. In April 2023, for example, NBMA displayed the application by the **Institute of Agricultural Research (IAR), Samaru, Zaria** for general release of GM cowpea Event 245F with the Cry2Ab gene for Maruca pod borer resistance. The notice ran for 21 days, from 6 to 26 April 2023, and asked for comments to be sent to the Director-General by email.

blocks.title: Path of a release application
blocks.caption: The public display is your formal chance to be heard before a release decision.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a comment on a display notice
blocks.context: For example, Funmi chairs a farmers' cooperative in Ogun. A new notice appears on the NBMA website with a 21-day display that opens on a Monday, 3 March. She wants the cooperative's comment in on time.
steps: Day 1 is 3 March, so day 21 is 3 + 20 = 23 March. That is the last day to submit.
She sets an internal deadline 3 days earlier, 20 March, to allow for network problems.
Week 1 (3 to 9 March): she downloads the notice and reads the summary with two members.
Week 2 (10 to 16 March): the cooperative meets and writes its questions, for example on refuge rules and seed availability.

Week 3 (17 to 20 March): she types a short, polite comment naming the application, the cooperative and its specific questions, and sends it to the email address in the notice, keeping a screenshot of the sent message.
blocks.result: The comment is sent on 20 March, three days before the 23 March deadline, with a clear record of what was sent and when.

blocks.text: How to write a useful comment

A comment is most useful when it is specific and polite. Name the application exactly as it appears in the notice. Say who you are, for example a cooperative of cowpea growers. Then ask clear questions or raise concerns that the regulator can act on, such as how refuge rules will be explained to smallholders, where certified seed will be sold, or how farmers will report problems. Avoid general statements such as "we reject GMOs" or "we support science" with no reasons, because they give the reviewers nothing to examine.

Keep a copy of everything you send, and note the date and time. If you receive a reply, file it with your notes. This record shows your group took part in the process and helps you follow the decision when it is published.

blocks.title: Check the source, then check the date
blocks.text: Approval status changes. Before you repeat a claim about what is approved or banned, look for the regulator's own notice and note its date. Use the NBMA website for Nigeria and the Biosafety Clearing-House for other countries that are Parties to the Protocol.

Other agencies also play roles around GM products in Nigeria, for example in seed certification and food registration. When you are unsure which body handles a question, ask NBMA or your state agricultural extension office directly and write down the answer, the person and the date.

takeaways: The Cartagena Protocol (adopted 29 January 2000) covers living modified organisms and created the Biosafety Clearing-House.
Codex texts guide food safety assessment; labelling rules differ by country.
Nigeria's regulator is the National Biosafety Management Agency, under the NBMA Act 2015.
Release applications go on public display, and citizens can comment before the deadline.

activity.title: Find the current position
steps: Visit the NBMA website and find its most recent public display notice or news item about a GM crop.
Write down the crop, the applicant, the trait, the dates and how comments are sent.
Count the days in the display period and set yourself an internal deadline 3 days earlier.
Check one legal claim from your claims log against what you found and record the result with the date.
activity.evidence: Your notes on the notice with dates, your deadline calculation and the updated claims log entry.

quiz.q: In a compositional comparison, a GM maize has 9.4 g protein per 100 g and its comparator has 9.0 g. The normal range for ordinary maize is 6.0 to 12.0 g. What is the best conclusion?
options: The GM maize is unsafe because it differs
The comparator is wrong and must be replaced
The difference is about 4.4 percent and inside the normal range, so it is not a concern on its own
Protein cannot be measured in GM crops
quiz.explain: 0.4 divided by 9.0 is about 4.4 percent, and 9.4 g lies inside 6.0 to 12.0 g. Differences matter when they are large, outside natural variation or biologically meaningful.

quiz.q: Which statement matches WHO's guidance on GM food?
options: All GM foods are safe forever
GM foods have been proven to cause infertility
GM foods currently on the international market passed safety assessments and are not likely to present risks for human health
quiz.explain: This is WHO's stated position. It applies to foods that passed assessment, and WHO says each GM food should be assessed case by case.

quiz.q: A farmer's Bt seed leaflet requires a refuge of 10 percent. Her cowpea area is 15,000 square metres. How large is the refuge?
quiz.explain: 10 percent of 15,000 is 0.10 x 15,000 = 1,500 square metres, leaving 13,500 square metres for Bt cowpea.

quiz.q: Why does a refuge slow the evolution of resistance in pests?
options: It kills all insects in the area
It produces susceptible insects that mate with rare resistant survivors from the Bt field
It makes the Bt protein stronger
quiz.explain: Susceptible insects from the refuge dilute resistance genes. Without them, resistant survivors mate with each other and resistance spreads quickly.

quiz.q: Which body regulates the release of GMOs into the environment in Nigeria?
quiz.explain: NBMA, established under the NBMA Act 2015, regulates the release, handling and use of GMOs in Nigeria.

quiz.q: An NBMA public display opens on 10 June and runs for 21 days, counting 10 June as day 1. What is the last day to comment?
quiz.explain: Day 21 is 10 + 20 = 30 June. June has 30 days, so 30 June is the last day.

modules.title: Checking Claims and Leading Balanced Conversations
modules.overview: This module turns knowledge into community leadership. You will use a scoring method to test any GMO claim, plan and run a respectful community conversation, and complete a project that documents your country's regulatory position, one evaluated claim and a communication plan.

lessons.title: A five-question method for testing any GMO claim
objectives: Apply five questions to any GMO claim and score its credibility
Recognise common warning signs of misinformation in either direction
Rank sources from strongest to weakest for each type of claim
Write a short, fair verdict on a claim with the evidence you used

blocks.text: In Module 1 you started a claims log. Now you will test those claims with one repeatable method. The aim is not to win arguments. It is to reach a fair verdict you can explain, and to be honest when the answer is "partly true" or "not yet known".

blocks.name: right-pointing-magnifying-glass
blocks.caption: Every claim gets the same five questions, whichever side it favours.

blocks.text: The five questions

blocks.title: Five questions for any claim
items: Is it about here and now?
blocks.caption: Score each question 0, 1 or 2, for a total out of 10.

items: **What exactly is claimed?** Rewrite it as one clear sentence. Vague claims such as "GMOs are poison" do not name a crop, event or effect. Score 2 if specific, 1 if partly, 0 if vague.
**Which type?** Food safety, environment, economics or law. Score 2 if the evidence offered matches the type, 0 if it does not, for example a seed price used to prove a health danger.

**Who is the source?** Score 2 for a regulator, WHO, FAO, Codex or a named peer-reviewed study, 1 for a named expert or reputable news report that cites one, 0 for an anonymous forward or a seller of a competing product.
**What evidence is shown?** Score 2 if you can follow it to the original document, 1 if it is described but not linked, 0 if none.
**Here and now?** Score 2 if it concerns an approved product in your country and is current, 1 if it is from elsewhere or old, 0 if it describes something not present here.

blocks.text: A total of 8 to 10 suggests a credible claim, 4 to 7 means partly supported and needs more checking, and 0 to 3 means do not repeat it. The score guides your judgement; it does not replace it.

blocks.title: Worked example: scoring two claims fairly
blocks.context: For example, Chioma, a nurse in Port Harcourt, scores two messages from her church WhatsApp group: one against GMOs and one in favour.
steps: Claim 1: "GM foods cause cancer, a doctor said so." Specific? Partly, no crop named: 1. Type match? No evidence offered of any kind: 0. Source? An unnamed doctor: 0. Evidence? None: 0. Here and now? Not linked to any product in Nigeria: 0. Total: 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 1 out of 10.

Claim 2: "GM cowpea will end hunger in Nigeria." Specific? Names a crop but 'end hunger' is vague: 1. Type match? An economic and food security claim with no yield or price data: 0. Source? A seed advert: 0. Evidence? None: 0. Here and now? Relates to a crop discussed by Nigeria's regulator: 2. Total: 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 3 out of 10.
She compares both with WHO's statement on approved GM foods and with NBMA's published notices.

She writes a verdict for each: Claim 1 is not supported by WHO's assessment of approved foods. Claim 2 overstates what one pest-resistance trait can do; hunger also depends on prices, storage, income and conflict.
blocks.result: Both claims score 3 or less, so Chioma does not forward either. She posts one calm message with WHO's statement and a link to NBMA's website.

blocks.text: Use the score honestly when you like the conclusion. It is tempting to give a friendly claim an extra point. If you notice yourself doing this, score the claim again as if it came from someone you disagree with.
Warning signs on both sides

head: Warning sign
Anti-GMO example
Pro-GMO example
rows: Herbal cure promising to "clean GMO from your body"
Unlabelled seed sold as "the new GM super seed"
A company's market share used to prove a health effect
A yield figure used to dismiss environmental concerns

blocks.title: Scams use GMO fears and hopes
blocks.text: Be careful with anyone selling a test kit to "detect GMO" in your food at home, a remedy to "remove GMO from your body", or seed claiming to be an approved GM variety outside a registered dealer. Do not send money or personal details. Ask NBMA or your extension office first.
Writing a fair verdict

A good verdict has three parts: what the claim says, what the best evidence shows, and what remains uncertain. For example: "The claim says GM cowpea harms bees. NBMA's process includes environmental assessment, and Cry2Ab targets certain caterpillars, not bees. I did not find a published study on bees and this cowpea, so I will ask the extension office." That verdict is honest about what you found and what you did not.

takeaways: Use five questions: what, type, source, evidence, here and now.
Score each 0 to 2; 0 to 3 means do not repeat the claim.
Absolute words, miracle or fear language and missing sources are warning signs on both sides.
A fair verdict states the claim, the best evidence and what is still uncertain.

activity.title: Score three claims
steps: Pick three claims from your claims log, at least one favouring GMOs.
Score each with the five questions and add up the totals.
Write a three-part verdict for each claim.
Note one claim you could not resolve and the expert or office you will ask.
activity.evidence: Your three score sheets with totals and written verdicts.

lessons.title: Running a balanced community conversation on GM food and farming
objectives: Plan a timed 30-minute community session on GMOs
Use listening and questioning techniques that lower defensiveness
Separate settled points from open questions when you speak
Respond to a strongly held view without shaming the person

blocks.text: Facts alone rarely change minds. People hold views on food because they care about their children's health, their money and their land. A good facilitator respects that care first, then helps the group look at evidence together. This lesson gives you a plan you can run in a cooperative meeting, a church women's fellowship or a market association.

blocks.name: public-discussion
blocks.alt: People sitting together in a group discussion
blocks.caption: A balanced conversation lets people voice concerns before evidence is shared.

blocks.text: Three principles

items: **Listen before you explain.** Ask what people have heard and what worries them. Write their concerns where all can see.
**Sort before you answer.** Group concerns into the four types: food safety, environment, economics, law. Many arguments disappear once people see they are talking about different questions.

**Say what is settled and what is open.** Settled: WHO's position on approved GM foods, the fact that Nigeria has a biosafety regulator. Open: whether a particular variety will pay on a particular farm, how well stewardship will be followed, how seed supply will work over time.

blocks.title: A 30-minute session
blocks.caption: Each stage has a time limit so the session stays practical.

blocks.title: Worked example: timing a session
blocks.context: For example, Grace leads the monthly meeting of a 25-member women farmers' cooperative in Plateau. She has 30 minutes on the agenda.
steps: Welcome and ground rules (one person speaks at a time, no insults): 3 minutes.
Collect what people have heard, written on a flip chart: 7 minutes.
Sort concerns into the four types together: 5 minutes.
Share checked facts, using printed WHO and NBMA statements: 6 minutes.
Discuss open questions such as seed cost and refuge rules: 6 minutes.
Agree next steps, for example inviting an extension officer: 3 minutes.
Check the total: 3 + 7 + 5 + 6 + 6 + 3 = 30 minutes.
blocks.result: Grace has a plan that fits exactly into 30 minutes and gives the group more time to talk (7 + 5 + 6 + 3 = 21 minutes) than she spends presenting facts (6 minutes).

blocks.text: Before the session

Preparation matters as much as the meeting itself. Agree the time slot with the group's leader so you are not squeezed into the last five minutes. Print your handout the day before. Check the NBMA website again so your facts are current, and write the date you checked on the handout. If you plan to invite an extension officer or a teacher, confirm in writing and tell them which questions the group is likely to ask.

Think about language and setting too. In many groups, a session in Hausa, Igbo, Yoruba, Pidgin or another local language will reach more people than one in English. Choose simple words for technical terms, for example "a gene is one recipe in the plant's instruction book". Seat people in a circle if you can, so it feels like a conversation rather than a lecture.
During the session

Write every concern on the flip chart in the speaker's own words, then ask the group to help place each one under food safety, environment, economics or law. When you share facts, read WHO's sentence aloud exactly as written and show NBMA's website on your phone. When you reach open questions, invite people who farm to speak first, because they know the local pest pressure, costs and seed supply better than anyone.
Phrases that help

head: Situation
Try saying
Avoid saying
rows: "That is a serious worry. Where did you hear it? Let us check it together."
You do not know the answer
"I do not know yet. I will ask NBMA or the extension office and report back."
"What problem on your farm would it solve, and what would it cost?"
"Let us keep to the question, not the person."

blocks.title: Print, do not just forward
blocks.text: Many members may have limited data or may not read long messages. A single printed page with WHO's safety sentence, NBMA's website address and the four claim types is easier to share than links. Write the date on it so people know when the information was checked.
When a view does not change

Some people will keep their view, and that is their right. Your goal is that they know where to check facts and that the group can discuss the topic without hostility. Respect choice where the law allows it: a consumer may choose to avoid a food, and a farmer may choose not to plant a variety. What the group should not do is spread false claims or plant unapproved seed.

blocks.title: Respect privacy
blocks.text: If someone shares a personal health situation during the session, do not repeat it outside the meeting or link it to GMOs without evidence. Encourage them to see a qualified health worker for any health concern.

takeaways: Listen first, sort concerns into four types, then share checked facts.
Say clearly what is settled and what is still open.
Give the group more time to talk than you spend presenting.
It is fine to say "I do not know yet" and report back.

activity.title: Plan your session
steps: Choose a real group you belong to and a date when you could hold a 20 to 30 minute session.
Write a timed plan and check that the minutes add up to your slot.
Prepare a one-page handout with WHO's safety sentence, the four claim types and NBMA's website address, dated.
Write answers to the two concerns you expect to hear most often.
activity.evidence: Your timed plan with the sum checked, and a photo of your handout.

lessons.title: Final project: your country brief, claim dossier and outreach plan
objectives: Research and document your country's current GMO regulatory position with dated sources
Produce a full evaluation of one GMO claim using the five-question method
Write a communication plan with audience, message, channel and timing
Set a 90-day plan to keep your knowledge current

blocks.text: Your final project brings the whole course together in three short documents. Together they show that you can find the facts for your own country, test a claim fairly and share balanced information with others. Keep each document to one or two pages so it is useful, not just long.

blocks.name: document-search
blocks.caption: A good brief rests on dated, checkable sources from the regulator and health bodies.

blocks.text: Part A: country regulatory brief

items: Name your country's biosafety law and regulator. For Nigeria: the NBMA Act 2015 and the National Biosafety Management Agency.
List any GM crops you can confirm from the regulator's own notices, with the trait, the applicant and the date of the notice.
Note how the public can take part, for example the public display of release applications.
Add the international layer: whether your country is a Party to the Cartagena Protocol, checked on the Biosafety Clearing-House.
Mark anything you could not confirm as "not confirmed" instead of guessing.

blocks.text: Part B: claim dossier

Choose one claim from your log that matters in your community. Write the exact wording and where you met it, the type, your five-question scores, the best sources you found, and a three-part verdict. Include what remains uncertain and who you asked.
Part C: outreach plan

Decide who needs balanced information most, for example a farmers' group considering new seed, or mothers worried about baby food. Choose one key message, the channel (meeting, printed sheet, WhatsApp voice note in a local language), the date, and how you will know it worked, for example the number of people who attended or the questions they asked.
Quality checks before you submit

items: Every fact in Part A has a source and the date you checked it.
Nothing is stated as approved, banned or safe unless a regulator or health body says so in its own words.
Part B gives the claim's exact wording and the five scores add up to the total you wrote.
Part C's session minutes add up to the time slot, and the measure of success is a number you can actually count.
Your language is plain enough for a member with limited schooling to follow when you read it aloud.

blocks.text: Share your draft with one person who disagrees with you about GMOs and ask whether it seems fair to them. You do not need their agreement, but if they can point to a sentence that overstates the case on either side, fix it. A brief that both a sceptic and an enthusiast accept as fair is far more useful to your community than one that only your own side trusts.

blocks.title: Your 90-day plan
blocks.caption: Rechecking at the end keeps your brief current, because approvals and rules change.

blocks.title: Worked example: a completed project summary
blocks.context: For example, Aisha is a cooperative secretary in Kaduna. She completes her project over 90 days and summarises it on one page.
steps: Part A: she records the NBMA Act 2015, NBMA's mandate, and the April 2023 public display of IAR Samaru's application for GM cowpea Event 245F with the Cry2Ab gene, with the notice link and the date she checked it.

Part B: she evaluates the claim "GM beans cause stomach ulcers". Scores: specific 1, type match 0, source 0, evidence 0, here and now 1. Total 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 2 out of 10. Verdict: no evidence given; WHO states approved GM foods passed safety assessment; she advises anyone with stomach pain to see a health worker.
Part C: she plans a 30-minute session for 40 members and a printed sheet in Hausa and English.
Result tracking: 32 of 40 members attend, which is 32 divided by 40 = 80 percent. They raise 9 questions; she answers 6 on the day and promises to report back on 3.
Day 90: she rechecks the NBMA website and adds any new notices to her brief with dates.
blocks.result: Aisha's project shows dated facts, a fairly scored claim and a measured outreach: 80 percent attendance and 6 of 9 questions answered on the spot, with the other 3 followed up.

blocks.text: After the project, keep the habit going. Add new claims to your log as you meet them, score them the same way, and recheck the regulator's website every few months. Your three documents become a living reference that you can update, print and share whenever the topic returns in your community.

blocks.title: Keep it honest
blocks.text: Do not present your project as official advice. Say clearly that it is a summary prepared for learning and community discussion, list your sources, and invite people to check the regulator's website for the latest position.

When you finish, you will be able to do something many people cannot: talk about GMOs calmly, separate the questions, point to real sources and admit what is still uncertain. That is the skill your community needs, whichever way individual choices go.

takeaways: Part A documents your law, regulator and confirmed notices, with dates.
Part B scores and judges one real claim with a three-part verdict.
Part C sets audience, message, channel, date and a simple measure of success.
Recheck the regulator's website at the end, because approvals change.

activity.title: Start your project
steps: Open three documents or notebook sections titled Part A, Part B and Part C.
Fill in the law and regulator for your country in Part A with the date you checked.
Copy the claim you will evaluate into Part B, word for word.
Write the date of your planned outreach session in Part C and the measure you will use.
activity.evidence: Photos or screenshots of the three started sections with dates.

quiz.q: A message says 'Studies show GMOs are dangerous' with no link, no crop named and no author. Using the five-question method, what should she do?
options: Forward it because studies were mentioned
Ask the sender to forward it to more people
Score it low for vagueness, no source and no evidence, and not repeat it
quiz.explain: It names no crop, no source and no checkable evidence, so it scores near 0. A low score means do not repeat it until real evidence appears.

quiz.q: Which of these is a warning sign of misinformation in favour of GMOs?
options: Claiming one GM seed will end all hunger
Quoting WHO's statement word for word
Linking to an NBMA public notice
Saying some questions are still open
quiz.explain: Miracle language and absolute promises are warning signs whichever side they favour. Hunger depends on many factors beyond one trait.

quiz.q: A facilitator has a 25-minute slot: welcome 2, collect views 6, sort concerns 5, share facts 5, discuss open questions 5. How many minutes are left for agreeing next steps?
quiz.explain: 2 + 6 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 23 minutes, so 25 minus 23 = 2 minutes remain for next steps.

quiz.q: During a session, a member asks a question you cannot answer. What is the best response?
options: Say you do not know yet, and that you will ask NBMA or the extension office and report back
Tell her the question is not important
quiz.explain: Admitting uncertainty and following up with a credible source builds trust and avoids spreading a guess as fact.

quiz.q: Which item belongs in Part A, the country regulatory brief?
options: Your personal opinion of seed companies
A list of rumours from WhatsApp
Prices you guessed for GM seed
The name of the biosafety law and regulator, with dated notices you confirmed
quiz.explain: Part A records verifiable facts: the law, the regulator and confirmed notices, each with a date and source.

quiz.q: In an outreach session, 27 of 36 invited members attend. What is the attendance rate?

finalQuiz.q: Which change makes an organism a GMO under the WHO definition?
options: Crossing two maize varieties by hand pollination
DNA altered in a laboratory in a way mating and natural recombination cannot achieve
Selecting seed from the healthiest plants
finalQuiz.explain: WHO defines GMOs by the method of change: DNA altered in a way that does not occur naturally by mating or natural recombination.

finalQuiz.q: What is the job of a promoter in a gene construct?
options: It removes the gene after harvest
It acts as the on-switch that controls where and how strongly the gene is used
finalQuiz.explain: The promoter is the control signal that tells the plant cell when, where and how much to use the trait gene.

finalQuiz.q: A GM line is 87.5 percent local DNA on average. What will it be after one more backcross to the local variety?
finalQuiz.explain: The non-local share halves: 12.5 percent becomes 6.25 percent, so the line becomes 93.75 percent local.

finalQuiz.q: Someone says, 'GM maize is illegal in Nigeria.' Which type of claim is this and where should it be checked first?
options: Legal; the National Biosafety Management Agency's own notices
finalQuiz.explain: It is a legal and policy claim, so the regulator's published decisions and notices are the right first source.

finalQuiz.q: In Codex-style safety assessment, what is the 'comparator'?
options: The conventional version of the same crop with a history of safe use
finalQuiz.explain: The GM crop is compared with its conventional counterpart, grown side by side, to find and examine any meaningful differences.

finalQuiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the areas WHO lists for GM food safety assessment?
finalQuiz.explain: WHO lists toxicity, allergenicity, specific components, gene stability, nutritional effects and unintended effects. Profit is an economic question, not a food safety one.

finalQuiz.q: A stewardship leaflet requires a 20 percent refuge. A farm has 3 hectares (30,000 square metres) of the crop. How much Bt crop can be planted?
finalQuiz.explain: Refuge = 0.20 x 30,000 = 6,000 square metres, so Bt area = 30,000 minus 6,000 = 24,000 square metres.

finalQuiz.q: Conventional seed costs N30,000 and needs 5 sprays at N10,000 each. GM seed costs N50,000 and needs 2 sprays at N10,000 each. Using these illustrative figures, which is cheaper for seed plus spraying and by how much?
finalQuiz.explain: Conventional: 30,000 + 50,000 = N80,000. GM: 50,000 + 20,000 = N70,000. GM is cheaper by N10,000 with these numbers, and the answer changes if spray numbers change.

finalQuiz.q: What did the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety establish to help countries share information?
finalQuiz.explain: The Protocol, adopted on 29 January 2000, created the Biosafety Clearing-House and an advance informed agreement procedure for imports of living modified organisms.

finalQuiz.q: Why does NBMA put release applications on public display?
options: To announce that approval is already final
Because the NBMA Act 2015 requires public display so citizens can give input before a decision
finalQuiz.explain: The Act requires public display of applications to intentionally release a GMO, so the public can comment, as in the 21-day display for cowpea Event 245F in April 2023.

finalQuiz.q: A claim scores 1, 0, 0, 0, 2 on the five questions. What should she do?
options: Not repeat it; a total of 3 out of 10 means it is not supported
Share it widely; it scored 2 on one question
Treat it as credible because the total is above 0
Ignore the scoring and decide by feeling
finalQuiz.explain: 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 3 out of 10, which falls in the 0 to 3 band: do not repeat the claim until better evidence appears.

finalQuiz.q: In a community session, a member insists she will never eat GM food. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Tell her she is wrong and uneducated
Respect her choice, make sure she knows where to check facts, and keep the discussion respectful
Promise her GM food has no risks of any kind
finalQuiz.explain: The aim is informed, respectful discussion. Consumers may choose what to eat; the facilitator avoids both shaming and overstated promises.

capstone.title: GMO Literacy and Local Context Project
capstone.brief: Produce a three-part project: a dated brief on your country's GMO regulatory position and any confirmed GM crop notices, a documented evaluation of one specific GMO claim using the five-question method and credible sources, and a plan for communicating balanced, accurate information in your community.
steps: Write Part A: name the biosafety law and regulator, list GM crop notices you confirmed from the regulator's own website with dates, and note how the public can take part.
Check your country's status on the Biosafety Clearing-House and add the date you checked.
Write Part B: pick one claim from your claims log, score it with the five questions, list sources and write a three-part verdict.
Write Part C: choose an audience, one key message, a channel, a date and a measure of success, with a timed session plan whose minutes add up.
Run the session or share your printed sheet, then record attendance, questions asked and follow-ups promised.
On day 90, recheck the regulator's website and update Part A with any new notices.
evidence: Part A brief with every fact sourced and dated, and unconfirmed items marked
